editorial.headline: Designing the Domestic Objects That Shape Everyday Life
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet a Bali-wide PMA moratorium prevents registration there for the activity’s recorded risk class.
editorial.body:
This activity covers industrial design for household equipment and furniture: the practical and decorative objects that populate kitchens, bedrooms, dining spaces and living areas. Its scope reaches from glassware, tableware, cooking, serving and food-storage products to fireplace accessories, beds, tables, chairs and storage furniture. It also includes mirrors and frames, clothes hangers, curtains and blinds, wall and table ornaments, vases and pots, medals and belts, flags and festival decorations, and artificial flowers, fruit and plants. The design work may be carried out using specialised software.

The breadth matters. This is not a narrow label for one furniture type or one decorative object; it is an activity category for designing a wide field of domestic and furnishing products. A registered business can operate at Micro, Small, Medium or Large scale. That gives the category room for practices whose work ranges across functional household goods and furniture, while keeping the defining activity clear: industrial design for the products specified in the scope.

Nationally, the position is direct. Foreign investment is permitted for the activity, and foreign ownership may reach 100%. Put plainly, the national record allows this activity to be wholly foreign-owned. That is the national setting founders should begin with, but it is not the complete location-specific answer for Bali.

In Bali, a foreign-owned registration cannot be made for this activity today. The Bali record classifies it as blocked by risk class: at the Large scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every listed scope, and the activity is therefore caught by Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. The distinction is consequential rather than technical: national openness and a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remain part of the record, while Bali’s local moratorium prevents PMA registration for this activity there.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk activities.
